paragraphs.heading: A war between two alliances
paragraphs.text: World War I, also called the Great War, ran from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918. It was fought across the globe by two coalitions: the Allies, also known as the Entente, and the Central Powers. Between 15 and 22 million people died, counting the victims of war crimes and genocides, which places it among the deadliest conflicts ever. The war also helped the Spanish flu pandemic to spread.

paragraphs.heading: How Europe got there
paragraphs.text: For much of the 1800s the big European powers kept an uneasy balance, called the Concert of Europe. After France lost the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871, Otto von Bismarck was able to consolidate a German Empire, and France set out to get revenge for that defeat. Germany and Austria-Hungary formed the Dual Alliance in 1879, and when Italy joined in 1882 it became the Triple Alliance. On the other side, France allied with Russia in 1894 and reached the Entente Cordiale with Britain in 1904, and a deal between Britain and Russia in 1907 completed the Triple Entente.

paragraphs.heading: Ships and rivalry
paragraphs.text: Germany's economy and industry kept growing fast after 1871. With the backing of Kaiser Wilhelm II, Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz wanted to turn that wealth into a navy able to rival Britain's Royal Navy. The causes of the war included the rise of the German Empire, which upset Europe's old balance of power, along with sharper imperial rivalries shown in new alliances and an arms race.

paragraphs.heading: The spark in 1914
paragraphs.text: Trouble in the Balkans came to a head on 28 June 1914, when a Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip assassinated Franz Ferdinand, who was next in line for the Austro-Hungarian throne. Austria-Hungary held Serbia responsible and declared war on 28 July, and Russia mobilised to defend Serbia. Early in August, Germany declared war on both Russia and France. Britain joined once Germany invaded Belgium.

paragraphs.heading: Stalemate in the trenches
paragraphs.text: Germany hoped to knock France out quickly, but its advance was stopped in September 1914. In the west the fighting then settled into an almost unbroken line of fortified trenches. Huge battles at Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele did not break the deadlock there. In the east the front moved more, yet neither side won a decisive edge despite expensive attacks.

paragraphs.heading: How the war ended
paragraphs.text: The United States joined the Allies in April 1917 after Germany resumed all-out submarine attacks on Atlantic shipping. Later that year the Bolsheviks took power in Russia, which then made a separate peace with the Central Powers in March 1918. A German spring offensive that month won ground at first but wore out its army, and the Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August 1918 made the German front collapse. With revolution breaking out at home, Kaiser Wilhelm II gave up the throne on 9 November, and the Armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting.

paragraphs.heading: A new map of Europe
paragraphs.text: At the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 to 1920 the winners imposed terms on the losers. The Treaty of Versailles took territory from Germany, disarmed it and made it pay large reparations to the Allies. The Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires all fell apart, and new countries appeared, among them Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. The League of Nations was set up to keep the peace, but its failure to handle the unrest between the wars helped bring on World War II in 1939.
